news.title: How much of a repair we leave showing
news.summary: Why we do not hide a sashiko repair, and what we decide before any thread goes in.
news.body:
Mending is not restoration. Once a garment has a hole in it, the choice is not between damaged and new — it is between one kind of visible history and another.

What we decide first

Before any thread goes in, we decide whether the repair is structural or cosmetic. A thinning elbow that will tear within a season gets a backing cloth and a run of sashiko stitching. A small pinhole that has been stable for thirty years usually gets nothing at all.

Where we do stitch, we use indigo or ecru cotton, close to the cloth but not hidden in it. You should be able to find the repair with your eye, because you will find it with your hand anyway.

The listing says which repairs are ours and which came with the garment. We leave an earlier owner's work in place when it is sound. Quite often it is better than ours.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoTitle: How much of a repair we leave showing | TSUMUGI

news.title: A week in Hokkaido, looking for wool
news.summary: Five towns, what we looked at, and what we decided not to buy.
news.alt: Rail of wool coats in a shop
news.body:
Seven days, five towns, and one shop that had not been opened for two years. We came back with fourteen garments, which is fewer than the trip cost us.

Most of the week was spent not buying. A wool coat with a beautiful shoulder had been stored damp and smelled of it in a way that will not wash out. Two Norwegian sweaters had been mended with acrylic yarn, which we can undo, but not for what the seller wanted for them.

What we did take

Four sweaters from a closing outfitter, still carrying their paper size tags. A grey blanket coat with a broken pocket we can rebuild. And, from a man clearing his father's house, three field jackets he wanted explained to him before he would let them go.

They will appear here over the next month, once each has been washed, measured and photographed.

news.title: What a label tells you, and what it does not
news.summary: Union tags, care symbols and country marks — how far they narrow a date, and where they stop.
news.alt: Chambray shirt on a wooden hanger
news.body:
A label is the fastest way into a garment's history and the easiest way to be wrong about it.

Three things worth reading

  • Union labels: the design changed several times, so the tag itself brackets a period.
  • Care symbols: the standardised set arrived at different dates in different countries, which sometimes rules a decade out.
  • Country of manufacture: useful mainly as a pair with the brand — a maker moved production in a known year, and the label follows.

What a label will not tell you is the year. Stock sat in warehouses, and old labels were used up long after they were designed. A tag gives you a window, usually of five to ten years.

So we write what the label supports and nothing further. When the window is wide, the listing says so; when the tag is gone or unreadable, we write that the date is unknown. That is not a fault in the garment.
news.author: TSUMUGI Studio
news.seoTitle: What a label tells you, and what it does not | TSUMUGI

news.title: Photographing a garment in the colour it actually is
news.summary: Why we shoot by the window, and the rules we keep while doing it.
news.alt: Pale garments on a rail in daylight
news.body:
Every photograph here is taken by the north window on the second floor, between about ten in the morning and two in the afternoon. There is no flash and no continuous light.

Studio light sells clothes. It fills the weave, lifts faded cotton back towards a colour it no longer has, and flattens the shadow that tells you how heavy a cloth is. Window light is less flattering and more useful.

The rules we keep

  • One light source, and no reflector on the front.
  • White balance set from a grey card once per session, never per photograph.
  • No dodging, no added saturation, no removing marks — a stain that is in the garment is in the picture.

On a grey day we wait. It costs a day of listing, and it is the reason a parcel arrives looking like its photographs.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoTitle: Photographing a garment in the colour it actually is | TSUMUGI
news.seoDescription: Why we shoot by the window, and the rules we keep while doing it.

news.title: Washing a forty-year-old sweater
news.summary: Cold water, flat drying, and the decision not to wash at all.
news.body:
The damage we see most often is not moths. It is hot water, strong detergent and haste.

What we do here

Cold water, a neutral wool detergent, and thirty minutes of soaking rather than agitation. Lift the sweater out supporting the whole body — wet wool stretches under its own weight if you hold it by the shoulders. Press the water out in a towel; never wring it.

Dry flat, out of direct sun, and reshape it while it is still damp. Measure the chest and the sleeve before washing, then pull it gently back to those numbers.

Often the right answer is not to wash at all. A night in moving air clears most of what makes a garment smell old. We wash a piece once before it goes on the rail; after that we would rather you left it alone until it needs it.

news.title: Autumn arrivals from 12 September
news.summary: Sixty pieces, mostly outerwear, published from 11:00 on 12 September.
news.alt: Rail of garments in the shop
news.body:
Sixty pieces will be published from 11:00 on 12 September, in three groups through the day: outerwear first, then trousers, then knitwear and shirting.

Most of it came from two sourcing trips in June and July — field jackets, three waxed coats, and a run of Norwegian sweaters from a closing outfitter in Hokkaido.

Everything is one of one. Each piece is washed, measured and photographed before it appears, so listings go up as they are finished rather than all at once.

The shop is open the same day, Thursday to Sunday, 12:00—19:00, and anything published online can be seen on the rail.

news.title: Repair consultations — first Saturday of the month
news.summary: Bring one garment. We will look at it with you and say what can be mended.
news.alt: Sweatshirt and jeans laid out flat
news.body:
On the first Saturday of each month, from 13:00 to 17:00, bring one garment and we will look at it with you.

We will tell you what we would do, what we would leave alone, and roughly what it would cost. Small work — a seam, a button, a single hole — is usually done on the spot at no charge. Anything larger we quote, and you are free to take it elsewhere.

It does not have to be something you bought from us. No appointment is needed; if two people are already waiting, we may ask you to come back later in the afternoon.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoTitle: Repair consultations — first Saturday of the month | TSUMUGI

news.title: An unworn garment tells us the least
news.summary: Why deadstock leaves us with the least to describe.
news.body:
Deadstock is easy to sell and hard to describe. Nothing has happened to it yet, so there is nothing to report beyond the label and the measurements.

A worn garment tells you where its owner's hands went, which seam gave first, whether the cloth thinned before the stitching did. That is the information we can pass on: not that a piece is rare, but that it has already proved it lasts.

Where we do keep it

We take unworn pieces occasionally, when the cut or the cloth is worth seeing intact — a reference for what the same garment looks like before thirty years of use. The listing says plainly that it has not been worn.

But we would rather sell you the one with the mended pocket. It has answered a question the other one has not been asked yet.
news.author: R. Seo

news.title: We are looking for help with measuring and photography
news.summary: Two days a week at the Kirigaya shop: measuring, photography and record-keeping.
news.body:
Two days a week at the Kirigaya shop, Thursday and Friday, 11:00 to 18:00. The work is measuring, photographing and writing up new arrivals, alongside one of us.

No experience with vintage clothing is required. It helps if you are patient with a tape measure and comfortable writing plainly about condition.

Send a short email to hello@tsumugi.archive telling us what you wear most, and why. We reply to everyone.

This position has since been filled. Thank you to everyone who wrote.

news.title: August Arrivals
news.summary: Twenty-two pieces, most of them out of one house in Nagano, and two we sent back.
news.alt: Rail of vintage coats in warm daylight
news.body:
Twenty-two pieces this month. Most came from a single house in Nagano, cleared by a family who had kept everything: work coats, three generations of shirting, and a wardrobe of wool that had never been near a moth.

What we kept

The four indigo work coats are the reason we drove up. All four had been mended before, by hand, in a way that tells you the same person did it each time. We washed them and left every stitch where it was.

We also took a run of cotton shirting, ordinary in every respect except that it has been washed a few hundred times and is still square at the shoulder. That is not a thing you can go out and find on purpose.

What we sent back

Two coats had been stored in a shed, and the smell was in the wadding rather than on the cloth. Nothing we do here would have taken it out, so they went back with the rest of the house.

The pieces below went up first. The rest are on the rail at Kirigaya as they are finished.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoDescription: Twenty-two pieces, most of them out of one house in Nagano, and two we sent back.

news.title: July Arrivals
news.summary: Fourteen pieces out of the Hokkaido week, and the first of the winter knitwear.
news.alt: Cream knitwear on a wooden hanger
news.body:
Fourteen pieces, all of them from the week we spent in Hokkaido in June. They are the last of that trip — everything else is either sold or still waiting on a repair.

The knitwear

Four Norwegian sweaters from a closing outfitter, still carrying their paper size tags. They have never been worn, which is unusual for us, and each listing says so plainly: an unworn garment has less to tell you than a used one.

The grey blanket coat is the piece we would keep. Its pocket was rebuilt here, in cloth taken from inside the hem, and you can find the work if you look for it.

On sizing

Most of this month runs a size large against present-day labels. Every listing carries measurements taken flat; please read those rather than the tag.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoDescription: Fourteen pieces out of the Hokkaido week, and the first of the winter knitwear.

news.title: June Arrivals
news.summary: A quiet month: nine pieces, and the reason there were not more.
news.alt: Faded rust-coloured jacket on a plaster wall
news.body:
Nine pieces. Two buying trips came to nothing, and we would rather list nine garments we can describe honestly than thirty we cannot.

What did arrive is mostly summer cotton — fatigue trousers, two French work jackets with the maker's mark washed out of them, and a chambray shirt faded almost to white at the yoke.

On the repairs

Three of the nine reached us already mended, and all three were left as they were. The listings say which repairs came with the garment and which are ours.

The rest of the month went on photographing what was already here. It does not show from the outside, and it is most of the work.
news.author: R. Seo
news.seoDescription: A quiet month: nine pieces, and the reason there were not more.
